title: Italian Game for White
description: Learn the Italian Game with the white pieces: the Giuoco Piano plans, the Two Knights Defence, a short look at the Evans Gambit and a few traps to know.

moves.comment: The pawn takes space in the center and opens lines for the queen and bishop.
The knight develops and attacks the e5 pawn.
Black guards the pawn.
This is the Italian Game. The bishop looks straight at f7.

steps.intro: The idea: take the center, bring out your pieces, and aim your bishop at the weak f7 square.

moves.comment: The knight comes out and attacks e5.

hints: Use a knight.
Move the knight from g1 to f3.
steps.intro: White to move. Attack the e5 pawn and develop a knight.

hints: Start with the king's pawn.
Then bring out the knight.
Last, the bishop goes to c4.
steps.intro: Play the first moves of the Italian Game as White.

points: The idea in one line: grow the center, develop fast and aim at f7
Say each move out loud with its reason
The bishop on c4 is the signature piece of this opening
mistakes: Moving the same piece twice in the opening
Pushing the h-pawn or a-pawn because there is no plan
Forgetting that 3.Bc4 is a choice, not a rule
questions: Why does 1.e4 help our bishop and queen?
What does the knight on f3 attack?
Which black pawn does the bishop on c4 point at?

moves.comment: A quiet pawn move. It guards e4 and opens the c1 bishop.
White castles. The king is safe and the rook joins the game.

steps.intro: Here is a calm Italian setup. Count the pieces that are out: a knight and a bishop for White.

moves.comment: Castled. The king is tucked away and the rook is ready.

hints: Use your king.
Castle on the kingside: the king goes to g1.
steps.intro: White to move. Make your king safe.
Look at the position and think about the goal.
steps.question: What is a good goal for your first ten moves?
choices: Take many pawns with the queen
Move the same knight again and again
steps.explanation: Bring your pieces out, castle, and keep a pawn in the center.

points: Three goals: knights and bishops out, king castled, a pawn in the center
Count pieces developed after each move
Castling keeps the king safe and wakes up a rook
mistakes: Bringing the queen out early so it gets chased
Leaving the king in the center for many moves
Making a lot of pawn moves and few piece moves
questions: How many pieces have we developed so far?
Why do we castle before attacking?
Which piece should we develop next?

moves.comment: The bishop attacks f7.
A knight can join the bishop. Now two pieces aim at f7.

steps.intro: The f7 pawn is next to the king and is guarded only by the king. That makes it a target.

moves.comment: The bishop points at f7.

hints: Use your bishop.
Move the bishop from f1 to c4.
steps.intro: White to move. Develop the bishop so it aims at f7.
Look at Black's camp.
steps.question: At the start of the game, who guards the f7 pawn?
steps.explanation: Only the king guards f7 at the start. That is why it is a good target.

points: At the start only the king guards f7
The bishop and knight can both aim at it
Aiming is not the same as winning: build up first
mistakes: Capturing on f7 too early with the bishop
Sending the queen out to f7 alone
Defending with ...Qe7, ...Nf6 (blocks the f-file) or ...d5 (blocks the bishop)
questions: Which black piece guards f7 at the start?
Which of our pieces can attack f7?
Why is it better to wait before taking on f7?

moves.comment: This prepares a later d4 and makes a safe home for the pieces.
The e4 pawn is now protected.
The king is safe.
The rook backs up the e4 pawn.
If Black threatens the bishop it can retreat to b3 and stay on the same diagonal.
A small pawn move that stops a pin on the f3 knight.

steps.intro: The quiet plan: play c3 and d3, castle, and keep the pieces protected.

moves.comment: The quiet setup.

hints: Use a pawn.
Move the pawn on d2 to d3.
steps.intro: White to move. Protect the e4 pawn and open the c1 bishop with a quiet pawn move.

hints: After the bishop and knight are out, play the small pawn moves c3 and d3.
Castle, then put a rook on e1.
If the bishop is chased, go to b3.
steps.intro: Play the quiet Giuoco Pianissimo line as White.

points: This setup is called Giuoco Pianissimo, the very quiet game
Idea: build slowly, keep everything protected, make a plan later
Typical moves: c3, d3, castle, Re1, Bb3
mistakes: Playing d3 and then having no plan
Forgetting to castle
Letting the bishop get trapped: give it the b3 square
questions: What does the d3 pawn protect?
Where can the bishop go if a black pawn attacks it?
Why is a slow plan safe for beginners?

moves.comment: The big center push.
Recapture so White again has pawns on d4 and e4.
Black checks the king.
Block the check with the bishop.
Recapture with the knight, which develops a piece.

steps.intro: The bigger plan: play c3, then d4, to build two strong pawns in the center.

moves.comment: The center push.

hints: Use a pawn from the middle of your army.
Move the pawn on d2 two squares to d4.
steps.intro: White to move. Build a big center and attack e5 with a pawn.

moves.comment: A solid block.

hints: Use the bishop on c1.
Move it to d2 to block the check.
steps.intro: Black gave check with the bishop. Block it with your bishop.

points: Idea: two center pawns on e4 and d4 take space
If Black checks on b4, block and keep developing
This is the sharper plan; the quiet d3 plan is the calm one
mistakes: Moving the king after the check instead of blocking
Forgetting to recapture on d4 with the c-pawn
Pushing d4 before c3 is ready
questions: Why do we play c3 before d4?
What does a pawn on d4 control?
How can we answer a check on b4?

lessons.title: Do not rush to take f7

moves.comment: Check! But think about the trade.
The king simply takes the bishop. White gave a bishop for one pawn.

steps.intro: A common beginner mistake: take f7 at once. Here the bishop is lost for only one pawn.

moves.comment: Solid and good. The bishop stays on its fine diagonal.

hints: Use a pawn, not the bishop.
Move the pawn on c2 to c3.
steps.intro: White to move. Do not give the bishop away. Play the solid pawn move that prepares d4.

points: A bishop is worth more than one pawn
A quick sacrifice needs a clear follow-up
Stay calm: build first, attack later
mistakes: Playing Bxf7+ just because the move is a check
Giving up a good bishop for one pawn
Not asking what happens after the king takes
questions: What does White get for the bishop?
Does the king have to run away after Kxf7?
Which solid move would you play instead?

moves.comment: Black develops a knight and attacks e4.
The knight joins the bishop against f7.
Black's best idea: hit the bishop and block the diagonal.
White takes the pawn.

steps.intro: Black can answer 3.Bc4 with a knight. This is called the Two Knights Defence. White can play the sharp 4.Ng5 or the quiet 4.d3.

moves.comment: Two pieces now aim at f7.

hints: Use your knight.
Jump the knight from f3 to g5, aiming at f7.
steps.intro: White to move. Play the sharp move: a knight joins the bishop in the attack on f7.

hints: Develop the knight and the bishop first.
After 3...Nf6, jump the knight to g5.
Take the d5 pawn with the e-pawn.
steps.intro: Play the Knight Attack as White.

points: Black plays 3...Nf6 to hit the e4 pawn and develop
White can choose 4.Ng5 (sharp) or 4.d3 (quiet)
4.Ng5 attacks f7 but Black has good answers, so teach it as an idea, not a trick
mistakes: Playing 4.Ng5 and then moving the same knight again without a reason
Forgetting that after 4.Ng5 d5 Black fights back
Moving the queen out too early
questions: Which black pawn does the knight on f6 attack?
Why does the knight on g5 look at f7?
When would you pick the quiet 4.d3 instead?

moves.comment: Black takes back with the knight. This is the risky choice.
The Fried Liver idea: the knight takes f7.
The king takes the knight and steps out of its shelter.
A check that also attacks the knight on d5.
Another piece joins in. The black king is out in the open.

steps.intro: In this line White gives up a knight for a pawn to drag the black king into the open. Black can answer with care, so it is a sharp fight and not a sure win.

moves.comment: The knight takes the pawn and forks the queen and rook. Black will take it with the king.

hints: Use the knight that is already on g5.
Capture the pawn on f7.
steps.intro: White to move. Find the knight move at the heart of the Fried Liver idea.

moves.comment: Check, and the knight on d5 is attacked too.

hints: Use your queen.
Move the queen to f3. It gives check and also looks at the d5 knight.
steps.intro: The black king took on f7. White to move. Find the check that also attacks a knight.

points: This line is a sharp attack, not a guaranteed win
Black can avoid it with 5...Na5, shown in the next lesson
The point to teach: the black king gets pulled into the center
Do not memorize far, understand why the knight sacrifice is played
mistakes: Playing Nxf7 without seeing the follow-up check
Forgetting to bring the queen in with Qf3+
Trying this idea when Black has already avoided it
questions: Why is ...Kxf7 Black's best answer?
What does the queen check also attack?
What is White giving up, and what does White hope to get?

moves.comment: The bishop moves with check, so it is not lost.
The bishop retreats. White is a pawn up.
The knight returns, attacking e5.
The knight lands on a active central square.

steps.intro: Black can play 5...Na5 to hit the bishop and avoid the Fried Liver. White answers with a check.

moves.comment: The bishop escapes with check.

hints: Use the bishop that is being attacked.
Move it to b5 with check.
steps.intro: Black's knight attacks your bishop. Save it with a check.

points: After 4.Ng5 d5 5.exd5 the better black reply is 5...Na5, hitting the bishop
White answers with a check and stays a pawn up
Black gets quick development in return, so keep developing and castle
mistakes: Leaving the bishop to be taken on c4
Playing Bxf7+ in a hurry
Grabbing more pawns and forgetting to castle
questions: Why does the knight on a5 attack our bishop?
What does the check on b5 do for us?
How many pawns is White ahead?

moves.comment: The gambit pawn.
Black takes the pawn. Now White kicks the bishop with c3.
The pawn attacks the bishop and prepares d4.
The center grows.
Castle early.
Recapture and take the center back.
Another piece joins the game.

steps.intro: In the Evans Gambit White offers a pawn with b4. If Black takes it, White gets time to build a big center with c3 and d4.

moves.comment: The gambit. If the bishop takes, c3 comes next.

hints: Use a pawn from the side of the board.
Move the pawn on b2 to b4.
steps.intro: White to move. Offer a pawn to gain time with the Evans Gambit.

hints: The first gambit move is a pawn to b4.
After the bishop takes, play c3, then d4.
Castle, recapture on d4, then develop a knight.
steps.intro: Play the main Evans Gambit line as White.

points: A gambit means giving a pawn for a lead in development
The idea: after b4 and c3, White builds the d4 center with tempo
Teach this as an optional extra, not the main plan
Black can decline the pawn, we only study the accepted line
mistakes: Not following up with c3 and d4 after giving the pawn
Forgetting to castle quickly
Playing the gambit and then moving pieces twice
questions: Why does White give up a pawn?
What does c3 attack?
Which two pawns does White want in the center?

moves.comment: The knight takes a pawn. Black may think the queen is free.
Black takes the queen: a mistake.
Check from the bishop.
Checkmate! The bishop on f7 and the two knights close every escape.

steps.intro: This trap comes from the Philidor Defence (2...d6), but White's bishop is on c4 as in the Italian. Black's bishop on g4 pins the f3 knight to the queen, but the pin is not absolute, and that is the trap. White offers the queen and wins by checkmate in a few moves.

moves.comment: The knight takes the pawn.
Check!
Checkmate.

hints: Use the knight on f3.
...even though this lets the bishop take your queen.
Then check on f7 with the bishop, and finish with a knight move to d5.
steps.intro: White to move. Start the trap. Play the whole mating line. Black will take your queen on the way.

points: This is a trap for Black, who must not grab the queen
The trap comes from the Philidor Defence (2...d6), but White's bishop is on c4 as in the Italian
The bishop on g4 pins the f3 knight to the queen, but the pin is not absolute: the knight can still move, and that is the trap
Show that giving up the queen can lead to mate
If Black does not take the queen, White simply is a pawn up
mistakes: Taking the queen without checking what it allows
Pinning a knight but leaving the king boxed in
Playing the trap again and again against players who know it
questions: Which black move was the mistake?
Why can the king not run away at the end?
Which pieces make the final checkmate?

lessons.title: A trap: do not grab on f7

moves.comment: The knight takes a pawn. This is fine.
The queen attacks the knight on e5 and the pawn on g2.
The mistake. White takes again and attacks the queen and the rook, but forgets g2.
The queen takes g2 and hits the rook on h1.
The rook runs.
Check!
The final blunder. The bishop blocks, but 7.Qe2 would avoid the mate.
Checkmate! The knight checks and the king cannot escape.

steps.intro: This trap is for White to avoid. After 3...Nd4 safe moves are 4.Nxd4, 4.c3 and 4.O-O. 4.Nxe5 is fine too, but after 4...Qg5 White must not grab again with 5.Nxf7.

moves.comment: The queen takes the pawn and attacks the rook.
Check!
Checkmate.

hints: This is Black's turn, to see how the trap works. Use the queen.
Take the pawn on g2, then check on e4, then play a knight move to f3.
steps.intro: Black to move. White grabbed on f7. Find the line that ends in checkmate.

points: This is a trap against White, so teach what to avoid
After 3...Nd4 good answers are 4.Nxd4 exd4, 4.c3 and 4.O-O; 4.Nxe5 is also fine
The trap comes after 4.Nxe5 Qg5, when 5.Nxf7 is the mistake
The nickname is the Blackburne Shilling Gambit; the Lichess name is Blackburne-Kostić Gambit
Point out the mate on f3: the knight and queen work together
mistakes: Taking the e5 pawn without looking at the black queen and knight
Taking again on f7 after 4...Qg5
Moving the rook to f1 and missing the check on e4
Missing 7.Qe2, which avoids the mate
questions: Why is 4.Nxe5 tempting?
Which two black pieces make the final mate?
What safe moves can White play on move four?

moves.comment: Everything is protected and White has a clear setup.

steps.intro: The Italian Game is a good friend for beginners. The rules are simple: grow the center, develop your pieces, castle, then pick a plan.

moves.comment: Castled. Now plan Re1 and a bishop retreat to b3 if needed.

hints: Use your king.
Castle on the kingside: the king goes to g1.
steps.intro: White to move. Finish the quiet setup by making your king safe.
Think about the ideas, not the move list.
steps.question: What should you do first if Black plays a move you do not know?
choices: Go back to the ideas: develop, castle, protect the center
steps.explanation: The basic rules always help. Develop your pieces, castle and keep the center safe.

points: The Italian suits players who like open, natural play
It teaches the basic rules: develop, castle, fight for the center
Pick the quiet d3 plan for a calm game and the c3 and d4 plan for a sharper game
After 1.e4 e5 the Italian is just one of several good third moves
mistakes: Playing the same trap in every game
Learning long lines without knowing the plan
Forgetting that Black can choose other moves than the ones we studied
questions: What are the two main plans for White?
Which plan would you pick against a nervous opponent, and why?
What is the first thing to do if Black plays a move you do not know?
